messages.content: I keep writing «Ich sehe die Mann» and «Ich helfe den Mann». Why are both wrong in different ways?

Because the two verbs govern different cases, and masculine nouns are where German shows it. «sehen» takes the accusative: the man is the direct object, so «der Mann» becomes «den Mann» — «Ich sehe den Mann». «helfen» is one of the common verbs that take the dative instead: «Ich helfe dem Mann».

The feminine and neuter articles hide this in the accusative (die Frau, das Kind stay unchanged), which is why learners often only notice the system with masculine words. A useful core list of dative verbs: helfen, danken, gehören, gefallen, folgen, antworten (to a person). When in doubt, ask whether the verb means doing something TO someone as a recipient or beneficiary — German often marks that person with the dative even where English uses a plain object.
Erklär mir bitte den Unterschied: «Ich hänge das Bild an die Wand» und «Das Bild hängt an der Wand». Warum wechselt der Fall?

Das ist das Prinzip der Wechselpräpositionen. Bei «an» (wie auch in, auf, über, unter, vor, hinter, neben, zwischen) entscheidet die Frage: Wohin? oder Wo?

«Ich hänge das Bild an die Wand» — hier gibt es eine Bewegung mit einem Ziel, also Wohin? → Akkusativ: «an die Wand». «Das Bild hängt an der Wand» — das Bild bewegt sich nicht mehr, es ist einfach dort, also Wo? → Dativ: «an der Wand».

Vorsicht bei «hängen»: Das transitive Verb (etwas hängen) ist regelmäßig — «ich hängte, gehängt». Das intransitive (etwas hängt) ist stark — «das Bild hing». Im Alltag hört man oft nur den Fallwechsel; ein guter Test ist: Kann ich «wohin» fragen, ohne dass es komisch klingt? Dann Akkusativ.

In a formal report I need: 'Because of the weather, despite the rain, during the meeting, instead of the director...' — my dictionary gives wegen/trotz/während/statt with genitive, but my German colleague writes «wegen dem Wetter». Who's right?

Both, in different registers. The written standard takes the genitive: «wegen des Wetters», «trotz des Regens», «während der Sitzung», «statt des Direktors» (more formal still: «anstelle des Direktors»). In reports, exams, and official letters, use exactly that.

In everyday speech, «wegen dem Wetter» with the dative is extremely common and nobody will misunderstand you — but in writing it reads as careless. One more trap: with plural nouns that show no genitive ending, the dative is actually standard even in writing: «wegen der Kinder» can't take a visible genitive, so «wegen den Kindern» appears too. Rule of thumb: genitive in writing, dative tolerated in speech, and never «wegen» with a bare pronoun — it's «meinetwegen», «deinetwegen».
How do I keep «durch, für, gegen, ohne, um» straight? I have to write directions for a colleague visiting our office.

These five (plus «entlang», which is postposed) always take the accusative — no exceptions, which makes them the friendly prepositions. For your directions: «Gehen Sie durch den Haupteingang» (through the main entrance), «Der Besprechungsraum ist um die Ecke» (around the corner), «Das Formular ist für den Besucher» (for the visitor).

Two usage notes. «ohne» is followed by a bare noun more often than English expects: «ohne Mantel», «ohne mich!» — and «ohne zu» builds infinitive clauses: «Er ging, ohne sich zu verabschieden». And «für» with time means duration into the future («für zwei Wochen»), while «gegen» with clock time means approximately: «gegen 15 Uhr» = around 3 p.m., not against it.
«Kannst du mir helfen?» vs «Kannst du mich hören?» — I mix up mir/mich, dir/dich, ihm/ihn constantly. Is there a logic?

There is: the pronoun takes the case of its job in the sentence. «helfen» governs the dative, so the person helped is dative: «Kannst du mir helfen?», «Ich gebe dir das Buch», «Ich schreibe ihm». «hören» and «sehen» take the accusative: «Kannst du mich hören?», «Ich sehe dich», «Ich rufe ihn an».

The full set: nominative ich/du/er/sie/es/wir/ihr/sie — accusative mich/dich/ihn/sie/es/uns/euch/sie — dative mir/dir/ihm/ihr/ihm/uns/euch/ihnen. Notice «ihr» does double duty (nominative 'you-plural informal' and dative 'to her'), and formal «Ihnen» (to you) is always capitalised. A memory anchor: dative answers «wem?» (to/for whom), accusative answers «wen?» (whom, directly affected). Most everyday confusion is really verb government — learn the case with the verb, as one unit: «jemandem (Dat) helfen», «jemanden (Akk) anrufen».
My sentence: «Das ist der Freund, mit der ich ins Kino gehe.» Something's off — the relative pronoun after «mit»?

Yes: after a preposition, the relative pronoun must take the case the preposition demands. «mit» always governs the dative, and «der Freund» is masculine, so it has to be «mit dem»: «Das ist der Freund, mit dem ich ins Kino gehe.»

Relative pronouns copy the definite article's forms (der/die/das, den, dem, der, denen...), with two special genitive forms: dessen (masculine/neuter) and deren (feminine/plural) — «die Kollegin, deren Büro nebenan ist». The gender and number come from the noun referred to; the case comes from the pronoun's role inside the relative clause or from its preposition. Compare: «Das ist der Mann, den ich gestern sah» (accusative, object of sah) versus «Das ist der Mann, dem ich gestern geholfen habe» (dative, because helfen governs it).
Why does German say «der kleine Hund», «ein kleiner Hund», but «kleiner Hund» with no article? The adjective endings feel random.

They follow one principle: the case/gender signal must appear somewhere, ideally once. After the definite article, the article already shouts the information, so the adjective relaxes with weak endings: «der kleine Hund», «den kleinen Hund», «dem kleinen Hund» — mostly just -e or -en.

After «ein» (mixed declension), the ein-word carries the signal only sometimes: «ein kleiner Hund» (nominative masculine: ein shows nothing, so the adjective takes -er), but «einem kleinen Hund» (dative: einem shows it, adjective takes -en). With no article at all (strong declension), the adjective does all the work and copies the definite article's endings: «kleiner Hund», «kaltes Wasser», «mit frischem Brot». Learn it as a division of labour rather than three separate tables, and the system stops feeling random.
I'm reading a Munich rental ad: «3-Zi.-Whg., 78 m², NK 240 €, 3 MM Kaution, ab 1.3. frei, EBK, an ruhiges Paar zu vermieten.» Can you decode it?

Gladly — German rental ads are compressed to the edge of cryptography. «3-Zi.-Whg.» = 3-Zimmer-Wohnung, a three-room flat (rooms counted excluding kitchen and bath). «NK 240 €» = Nebenkosten, the monthly service charges on top of the cold rent (Kaltmiete); rent plus NK gives the Warmmiete. «3 MM Kaution» = a deposit of three Monatsmieten (monthly rents) — the legal maximum, normally three cold rents. «ab 1.3. frei» = available from 1 March. «EBK» = Einbauküche, a fitted kitchen is included, which matters because many German flats come with no kitchen at all. «an ruhiges Paar zu vermieten» = to let to a quiet couple.

Other abbreviations you'll meet constantly: «DG» Dachgeschoss (top floor), «EG» Erdgeschoss (ground floor), «Blk.» Balkon, «WBS» — a certificate of eligibility for subsidised housing, without which the flat isn't available to you at all.
What's the difference between «nach», «zu», and «in» for going places? I wrote «Ich fahre zu Berlin» and got laughed at.

The laughter was unfair, but the rule is clean. Cities, countries, and continents take «nach»: «Ich fahre nach Berlin», «nach Italien», «nach Hause» (home — fixed phrase). People, specific buildings, and institutions take «zu» plus dative: «Ich gehe zum Arzt», «zur Post», «zu meiner Schwester», «zum Bahnhof».

«in» plus accusative is for entering enclosed spaces and for countries with an article: «ins Kino», «in die Schweiz», «in die Türkei», «in die USA». And «bei» plus dative means at someone's place or workplace without movement: «Ich war beim Arzt», «Sie arbeitet bei Siemens». Quick grid: nach = named places on the map, zu = destinations with people or function, in = inside something, bei = already there.
Why does my sentence «Ich aufstehe um sechs Uhr» get corrected to «Ich stehe um sechs Uhr auf»? And in «Ich kaufe heute ein» — where did «einkaufen» go?

You've met separable verbs. Verbs like aufstehen, einkaufen, anrufen, fernsehen, umsteigen carry a prefix that detaches in main clauses: the verb stem takes the second position as usual, and the prefix is sent to the very end of the clause. «Ich stehe um sechs Uhr auf.» «Sie kauft heute im Supermarkt ein.»

The prefix rejoins in three situations: in the infinitive («Ich muss früh aufstehen»), in the perfect with ge- wedged inside («aufgestanden», «eingekauft»), and in subordinate clauses («..., weil ich früh aufstehe»). Practically: when you hear a lone «auf», «ein», «an», «mit», «vor» at the end of a German sentence, your ear should glue it back onto the verb at the front — the meaning often changes completely: «hören» is to hear, «aufhören» is to stop.
Ich muss einen Anruf bei einer Firma nachspielen. Was sage ich, wenn die Person nicht da ist, und was, wenn ich später noch einmal anrufen will?

Ein typischer Ablauf: «Guten Tag, hier spricht Jonas Weber von der Firma Klartext. Ich rufe wegen der Rechnung vom 3. Mai an. Könnte ich bitte mit Frau Lindner sprechen?» Ist sie nicht da: «Kein Problem. Könnten Sie ihr bitte ausrichten, dass ich angerufen habe? Ich rufe morgen Vormittag noch einmal an.» Oder formeller: «Ich rufe Sie später zurück» — Vorsicht, «zurückrufen» heißt: ich rufe die Person an, die mich angerufen hat.

Nützliche Bausteine: «Am Apparat» sagt die Person, die selbst gemeint ist («Ja, am Apparat»). «Bleiben Sie bitte kurz dran» = einen Moment warten. «Ich verbinde Sie» = ich stelle Sie durch. Und am Ende: «Vielen Dank für Ihre Hilfe. Auf Wiederhören!» — am Telefon sagt man Wiederhören, nicht Wiedersehen.
Explain this pair: «Ich fahre den Baum um» vs «Ich umfahre den Baum». One letter's stress can't really flip the meaning... can it?

It can, and this is the classic separable/inseparable trap. Stressed prefix = separable: «UMfahren» splits, so «Ich fahre den Baum um» means you knock the tree down by driving into it. Unstressed prefix = inseparable: «umFAHren» never splits, and it means you drive around the tree and avoid it. Same letters, opposite outcomes — one is an insurance claim, the other isn't.

Several prefixes live this double life: um-, durch-, über-, unter-, wieder-. «ÜBERsetzen» (separable) is to ferry across a river; «überSETZEN» (inseparable) is to translate. «WIEDERholen» (separable) is to fetch back; «wiederHOlen» (inseparable) is to repeat. In listening, the stress tells you which verb you have before the sentence even ends; in writing, watch whether the prefix separates in the sentence — that's your evidence.
Why do verstehen, besuchen, erklären, verkaufen never split? My list of prefixes feels like two families.

It is two families. Inseparable prefixes — be-, emp-, ent-, er-, ge-, miss-, ver-, zer- — are always unstressed and never detach: «Ich verstehe», «Sie besucht uns», «Er erklärt es», perfect without extra ge-: «verstanden», «besucht», «erklärt». Separable prefixes are stressed and mostly look like prepositions or adverbs: ab-, an-, auf-, aus-, bei-, ein-, mit-, nach-, vor-, weg-, zu-, zurück-.

The inseparable ones also shift meaning in ways you can't guess from the base verb: «kommen» is come, «bekommen» is receive; «stehen» is stand, «verstehen» is understand; «kaufen» is buy, «verkaufen» is sell (ver- often marks a transformation or a doing-away). Learn these verbs whole. The separable family, by contrast, is semi-transparent: «weggehen», «mitkommen», «nachschauen» behave predictably once you know the prefix's spatial sense.
It's my first day at a German engineering firm. The boss is Frau Dr. Berger, about 55. My team lead, Herr Yilmaz, is 30 and everyone seems casual. Who gets Sie and who gets du?

Default to Sie with everyone on day one, including Herr Yilmaz, and let the switch come to you. The convention: the senior person — by rank or by age — offers the du («Wir können uns gern duzen», or simply introducing herself: «Ich bin die Claudia»). Accepting is automatic; offering it upward yourself is the faux pas.

With Frau Dr. Berger, use «Guten Morgen, Frau Berger» — in most of Germany the title is used in address («Frau Dr. Berger») in formal introductions and letters, though in daily office speech many firms drop it after the first greeting; mirror what colleagues do. If you slip and say du to someone senior, don't panic: a brief «Entschuldigung — Sie, natürlich» and moving on is exactly how Germans handle it. Within a few weeks most modern teams land on du across the board, but the first move is never the newcomer's.
I need to email my professor and my study partner about the same missed seminar. Can one text serve both?

No — the same facts need two different shells. To the professor: «Sehr geehrte Frau Professorin Aydın, leider konnte ich am Dienstag nicht am Seminar teilnehmen, da ich krank war. Ein Attest liegt bei. Könnten Sie mir bitte mitteilen, welche Texte ich nacharbeiten sollte? Mit freundlichen Grüßen, Jonas Weber, Matrikelnummer 402…» Note the capitalised possessives — Ihre, Ihnen — whenever they refer to the person addressed with Sie.

To your study partner: «Hi Lena, ich war Dienstag krank und hab das Seminar verpasst. Kannst du mir deine Notizen schicken? Danke dir!» Trying to split the difference — «Liebe Frau Aydın» with du-verbs, or «Sehr geehrte» with a first name — is what actually sounds wrong. German marks the relationship in every verb and pronoun, so each message has to commit to one register from greeting to sign-off.
My Berlin gym instructor du's everyone, my Munich bank advisor Sie's me even after two years, and a startup founder I met used du in the first email. Is there a map for this?

There is a rough social map. Du is the default in sports clubs, gyms, universities among students, bars, startups, advertising, and most workplaces under about 40 — IKEA Germany famously addresses all customers with du. Sie remains standard in banking, insurance, law, medicine, administration, and any first contact with officials: the police officer and the clerk at the Bürgeramt get Sie, and they'll Sie you back, whatever your age.

The bank advisor isn't being cold — in finance, Sie is part of the professional product, and switching after two years would need an explicit offer, usually from her side. Regional colour: in rural Bavaria and Austria du spreads faster among neighbours, while Hamburg business culture keeps Sie longer. When genuinely unsure, Sie is the error that costs nothing; nobody is offended by respect, but premature du reads as either naive or pushy.
I accidentally said «Kannst du mir das bitte schicken?» to a long-standing client (we're on Sie terms). She went quiet for a second. How bad is it, and what do I do?

It's a small, recoverable slip — not a scandal. What she heard was a momentary over-familiarity, and the brief pause was likely just surprise. The clean repair is immediate, light, and once only: «Entschuldigen Sie — können Sie mir das bitte schicken?» Saying the corrected sentence itself is the apology; adding a smile and moving on signals it was a tongue-slip, not a demotion.

What not to do: apologise three times (that upgrades it into an incident), or laugh it off with more du. Context matters too: if you've worked together warmly for years, she may even take it as a cue — some clients respond «Wir können uns ruhig duzen», and then you accept gladly. But the offer must be hers. In writing the same slip looks worse, because it survives re-reading — proofread emails to Sie-contacts for stray du-forms and for lowercase «sie» where «Sie» is meant.
At a restaurant, is «Ich will das Schnitzel» rude? My textbook says «Ich hätte gern...» but I don't understand what that literally is.

«Ich will» isn't rude exactly, but it sounds like a demand from a child — adults soften it. «Ich hätte gern das Schnitzel» is Konjunktiv II of haben: literally 'I would like to have'. The unreal form signals 'this is a wish, not a claim', and that distance is the politeness. Equally natural: «Ich nehme das Schnitzel» ('I'll take...') or «Für mich bitte die Suppe».

The same softener runs the whole service encounter: «Könnte ich bitte die Karte haben?», «Wäre es möglich, noch Wasser zu bekommen?» And the staff use it back: «Hätten Sie gern einen Tisch am Fenster?» Learn «hätte gern + noun» as a single chunk for ordering anything, and «könnten Sie bitte...» for asking anyone to do anything — those two patterns carry most of polite daily German.
How do I turn these blunt sentences into polite Konjunktiv II requests? «Geben Sie mir den Bericht.» «Schicken Sie das heute.» «Helfen Sie mir.»

Three standard moves. (1) Modal in Konjunktiv II plus infinitive: «Könnten Sie mir bitte den Bericht geben?» «Würden Sie mir bitte helfen?» (2) A question frame: «Wäre es möglich, den Bericht heute zu bekommen?» (3) A wish statement: «Es wäre schön, wenn Sie das heute schicken könnten.»

Note the verb forms: könnte, würde, wäre, hätte — Konjunktiv II of können, werden, sein, haben. With most other verbs German prefers «würde + infinitive» («Würden Sie bitte anrufen?») rather than the rare one-word forms. Word order watch: in «..., wenn Sie das heute schicken könnten», the modal sits at the very end. None of this is more 'correct' than the imperative — «Geben Sie mir bitte den Bericht» with «bitte» is fine in a busy office. Konjunktiv II buys you warmth where the relationship is new, formal, or strained.
I want to say things like 'I wish I had more time' and 'If I were rich, I'd travel more' in German. My attempts sound like Google Translate word salad.

Two frames cover most wishes. For wishes about the present: «Ich wünschte, ich hätte mehr Zeit» — hätte is Konjunktiv II of haben; for being/states use wäre: «Ich wünschte, ich wäre jetzt am Meer.» For if-sentences: «Wenn ich reich wäre, würde ich mehr reisen.» The pattern is: wenn-clause with Konjunktiv II (verb at the end), main clause with würde + infinitive — or a one-word Konjunktiv II if the verb is haben/sein/modal: «Wenn ich mehr Zeit hätte, käme ich mit.»

Common learner errors: using würde in both halves («wenn ich würde...» is wrong), and using present tense in the wenn-clause for unreal situations (that's for real conditions: «Wenn es regnet, bleibe ich zu Hause» — rain is genuinely possible). Past unreal needs hätte/wäre + participle: «Wenn ich früher losgefahren wäre, hätte ich den Zug erreicht.»
I told my German host «Ich bin gestern ein Lehrer bekommen» trying to say 'I became a teacher yesterday'. She laughed for a full minute. What happened?

You said, roughly, 'I received a teacher yesterday' — bekommen means to receive or get (something handed to you): «Ich habe ein Paket bekommen», «Sie bekommt ein Baby». 'To become' is werden: «Ich bin Lehrer geworden.» Two traps in one verb family, because werden is also the future auxiliary and the passive auxiliary.

The wider false-friend cluster around it: «bekommen» ≠ become; «werden» ≠ worth; «bekommen» also does health duty — «Er hat eine Erkältung bekommen» (he caught a cold). And in restaurants you'll hear «Was bekommen Sie?» from staff, meaning 'What are you having?' — literally 'what do you receive'. File bekommen permanently under receive, and your host's laughter becomes a one-time tuition fee.
My colleague said «Das ist aktuell ein Problem» and «Mein Chef kocht heute». I translated both wrong. Help me untangle aktuell and Chef.

«aktuell» means current, at the moment — not 'actual'. 'The actual problem' in the sense of 'the real one' is «das eigentliche Problem» or «das wirkliche Problem». So your colleague said 'That's a problem right now', which is a statement about timing, not truth. Similarly «eventuell» means possibly, not eventually (that's «schließlich» / «am Ende»).

«Chef» is the boss, any boss: «meine Chefin» runs the department, she doesn't cook in it. A chef (cook) is «der Koch / die Köchin», and the head chef is «der Küchenchef». The sentence «Mein Chef kocht heute» most likely means the boss is cooking today — team lunch, perhaps — which is probably why it stuck in your mind. Both words are French loans that English borrowed with a narrower meaning than German kept.
Give me the dangerous false friends in one clinic: sensibel, brav, Gift, Rente, spenden, kontrollieren. I use at least three of them wrong.

One by one. «sensibel» = sensitive (easily hurt, delicate); English 'sensible' (reasonable) is «vernünftig». «brav» = well-behaved, obedient — a «braves Kind» sits still; 'brave' (courageous) is «mutig» or «tapfer». «Gift» is the lethal one: it means poison. A present is «ein Geschenk». Never announce you have «ein Gift» for someone's birthday.

«Rente» is a pension; rent for a flat is «die Miete». «spenden» is to donate (money, blood, organs); 'to spend' money is «ausgeben», time is «verbringen». «kontrollieren» is to check or inspect — the conductor «kontrolliert» your ticket; 'to control' in the sense of command is «steuern», «beherrschen», or «unter Kontrolle haben». These six are dangerous precisely because the sentences still parse — nobody notices the error except the meaning, which quietly walks off a cliff.
I'm moving to Vienna. My Berlin German keeps getting gentle corrections: Jänner, Erdapfel, Semmel... What's going on?

Austria keeps its own standard vocabulary, and it's official, not dialect — it appears in Austrian laws, menus, and schoolbooks. Months: Jänner (January), Feber (February). Food: Erdapfel (potato; Berlin: Kartoffel), Semmel (bread roll), Obers (cream), Marille (apricot), Ribisel (currant), Faschiertes (minced meat), Palatschinken (crêpes). A bag is «ein Sackerl», not «eine Tüte».

Greetings shift too: «Grüß Gott» is the normal polite hello in Austria and Bavaria, and «Servus» works for both hello and goodbye among acquaintances. You'll also hear «Bim» for the tram (from its bell). None of your Berlin words are wrong — Viennese understand everything — but adopting Jänner and Sackerl buys instant local credit. Switzerland is a separate case again; Austrian standard German is written with ß like Germany's, unlike Swiss spelling.
Working in Zurich next month. Why does Swiss written German look odd to me, and what words will catch me out in the office canteen?

The odd look is the missing ß: Swiss standard German abolished it, writing ss everywhere — «Strasse», «gross», «Grüsse». In speech, expect «Grüezi» (from 'Gott grüsse Sie') as the all-purpose polite greeting, «Grüezi wohl» to a group or very formally, and «Merci vielmal» for thanks — French loans are normal: Velo (bicycle), Billet (ticket), Poulet (chicken), Trottoir (pavement).

Canteen traps: «Znüni» is the mid-morning snack (from 'at nine'), «Zvieri» the afternoon one, «Zmorge» breakfast, «Znacht» dinner. «Rüebli» are carrots, «Härdöpfel» potatoes, and you «parkieren» a car rather than parken it. One caution: Swiss German dialects (Schwizerdütsch) dominate spoken life and differ sharply from standard German; colleagues will switch to Hochdeutsch for you, and understanding the dialect is a long-term project nobody expects of a newcomer.
Why does the same bread roll have five names on my Germany road trip — Brötchen, Semmel, Weck, Schrippe, Rundstück?

Because bread rolls are regional identity in edible form. Brötchen is the northern/central standard (and the word to use anywhere if unsure — it's understood nationwide). Semmel rules Bavaria and Austria. Schrippe is Berlin-Brandenburg. Weck (or Weckle) is the southwest — Baden-Württemberg and the Rhineland-Palatinate. Rundstück is Hamburg's local word.

Bakeries are where Germany's federal map is tastiest: the same trip also renames your jam doughnut (Berliner in the west, Pfannkuchen in Berlin itself, Krapfen in Bavaria/Austria) and your meatball (Frikadelle, Boulette, Fleischpflanzerl). Ordering with the local word is a small courtesy that staff genuinely notice. But don't overcorrect: nobody in Munich will blink at Brötchen; the variants are pride, not a test.
Translate 'It's not my cup of tea' and 'to break the ice' into German — and tell me which one survives literally.

Only one survives: «das Eis brechen» exists in German with exactly the social meaning — «Ein kleines Spiel am Anfang hat das Eis gebrochen.» German even has the noun «Eisbrecher» for an icebreaker activity.

'Not my cup of tea' does not survive at all — «Das ist nicht meine Tasse Tee» marks you instantly as a translator. Germans say «Das ist nicht mein Fall» (that's not my thing), «Das ist nicht so meins» (colloquial), or «Damit kann ich nichts anfangen». The pattern generalises: food-and-drink idioms are the least portable in any language, because they're anchored in national habits. Body and weather idioms travel better: 'to cross your fingers' fails too, though — Germans press thumbs: «Ich drücke dir die Daumen», and wishing luck with raised thumbs would be read as 'great!' instead.
My German friends keep using idioms I can't decode: «Tomaten auf den Augen haben», «Ich verstehe nur Bahnhof», «Das ist mir Wurst». Decode them and give me the English equivalents.

«Tomaten auf den Augen haben» — to have tomatoes on your eyes — means you're failing to see what's right in front of you; English would say 'Are you blind?' or 'It's staring you in the face.' «Ich verstehe nur Bahnhof» — 'I only understand train station' — is the German 'It's all Greek to me': total incomprehension, slightly self-mocking.

«Das ist mir Wurst» — 'that's sausage to me' — means 'I couldn't care less', equivalent to «Das ist mir egal» but jocular. Sausage is German's all-purpose indifference food (see also «Jetzt geht's um die Wurst» — now it's crunch time, literally 'now it's about the sausage'). Usage note: all three are colloquial and humorous; in a business meeting you'd choose the neutral versions. Idioms like these are best learned as recognition vocabulary first — using them slightly wrong sounds worse than not using them.
English borrowed Schadenfreude and Zeitgeist. What do Feierabend, Fernweh, and Weltschmerz actually mean — and why do people say they're untranslatable?

They're translatable as explanations, just not as single words. «Feierabend» is not 'evening' and not 'after work' — it's the culturally protected state of being done: «Ich mache jetzt Feierabend» closes the working day like a door, and emailing a German colleague deep into their Feierabend crosses a real line. «Fernweh» is the mirror of homesickness (Heimweh): an ache for faraway places you've perhaps never seen. «Weltschmerz» is world-weariness — a melancholy at the gap between how the world is and how it should be, a term from Romantic literature.

They feel untranslatable because German builds precise compound nouns where English needs a clause. But every language does this somewhere; the honest lesson is that compounds like «Verschlimmbesserung» (an improvement that makes things worse) or «Kopfkino» (the film playing in your head when you imagine scenarios) are productive patterns, not museum pieces — Germans coin new ones constantly.
Ich muss beim Arzt anrufen und einen Termin machen. Ich habe seit drei Tagen Halsschmerzen und leichtes Fieber. Was sage ich genau?

Ein natürlicher Anruf: «Guten Tag, mein Name ist Sarah Klein. Ich hätte gern einen Termin. Ich habe seit drei Tagen Halsschmerzen und leichtes Fieber.» Die Praxis fragt wahrscheinlich: «Sind Sie schon Patientin bei uns?» und «Worum geht es genau?» — dann: «Es geht um eine Erkältung, ich brauche auch eine Krankschreibung für meinen Arbeitgeber.»

Wichtige Vokabeln: «seit drei Tagen» (nicht «für drei Tage» — seit + Dativ für alles, was bis jetzt andauert), «Halsschmerzen» als ein Wort, «leichtes Fieber» (about 38°), «die Krankschreibung» = das Attest für den Arbeitgeber. In der Praxis selbst: «Ich warte dann hier?» — nein, Sie werden aufgerufen: «Frau Klein, bitte in Zimmer zwei.» Am Ende: «Gute Besserung!» ist der Standardwunsch — antworten Sie einfach «Danke schön!»
At Cologne station the announcement said: «Der ICE 782 nach München Hauptbahnhof hat voraussichtlich 20 Minuten Verspätung. Grund ist eine technische Störung am Zug.» What exactly did I just hear?

You heard: ICE 782 to Munich main station is expected to be 20 minutes late, due to a technical fault on the train. The vocabulary worth banking: «voraussichtlich» (expected/approximately — announcements hedge with it constantly), «Verspätung» (delay; the opposite is «pünktlich»), «Grund ist...» (the reason is...), «eine technische Störung am Zug» (a technical malfunction on the train itself).

Other announcement staples: «Wir bitten um Entschuldigung» (we apologise), «Der Anschluss nach Frankfurt wird erreicht / wird leider nicht erreicht» (your connection will / won't be held), «Bitte beachten Sie die geänderte Wagenreihung» (note the changed coach order — matters if you have a seat reservation), «Ein-, Ausstieg» at doors, and «Vorsicht an der Bahnsteigkante» (mind the platform edge). Deutsche Bahn also announces in English after the German — but the German comes first and contains the fuller detail.
My German CV says «Ich schrieb Berichte und leitete ein Team», but in interviews I catch myself saying «Ich habe Berichte geschrieben». Is one of them wrong?

Neither is wrong — they belong to different channels. Written German (CVs, reports, novels) uses the Präteritum: schrieb, leitete, entwickelte. Spoken German, especially in the south, runs on the Perfekt: «Ich habe Berichte geschrieben und ein Team geleitet.» In an interview the Perfekt sounds natural and the Präteritum sounds like you're reading aloud.

Exceptions in speech: sein, haben, and the modal verbs stay in Präteritum even when spoken — «Ich war Projektleiter», «Ich hatte drei Mitarbeiter», «Ich musste oft reisen» (nobody says «gewesen ist» or «gemusst habe» in conversation). Northern speakers use more Präteritum overall («Ich ging gestern...»), southerners less. For your interview: Perfekt for action verbs, Präteritum for war/hatte/modals, and your CV keeps the written style. That split is exactly what native speakers do unconsciously.
«Du musst das nicht machen» — my colleague meant I don't have to, but it sounds to me like 'you must not'. And how do I actually say 'must not'?

You've found one of German's most consequential traps, because it reverses English logic. «Du musst das nicht machen» = you don't have to do it (the necessity is negated). A prohibition is «Du darfst das nicht machen» — dürfen, not müssen, carries the 'must not': «Hier darf man nicht rauchen» (smoking is forbidden here), «Das darfst du nicht vergessen» (you mustn't forget that — note: it means it's important to remember!).

The pattern: nicht müssen = absence of obligation; nicht dürfen = presence of prohibition. English learners invert these for years because 'must not' looks like «musst nicht». Related pair: «Du brauchst nicht zu kommen» also means 'you needn't come' — brauchen + nicht works like müssen + nicht. When a German sign says «Betreten verboten» or «Rauchen nicht gestattet», that's the official prohibition register above both.
Why does «Ich fahre morgen mit dem Zug nach Berlin» put time, then transport, then place? In English I'd say 'I'm going to Berlin by train tomorrow' — the exact reverse.

German adverbial order follows TeKaMoLo: Temporal (when), Kausal (why), Modal (how), Lokal (where). «Ich fahre [morgen] [mit dem Zug] [nach Berlin]» — time, manner, place. English tends to run place-manner-time, so your instinct produces grammatically possible but foreign-sounding German like «Ich fahre nach Berlin mit dem Zug morgen».

Two saving graces. First, any one element can be fronted for emphasis, with the verb staying in second position: «Morgen fahre ich mit dem Zug nach Berlin.» Second, TeKaMoLo orders the middle field — after the verb — not the whole sentence; short pronouns jump ahead of full noun phrases («Ich gebe es ihm morgen»). In practice: when you build a long German sentence, stack when → why → how → where in the middle and you'll match native rhythm almost every time.
Restaurant scene: how do I ask for the bill, and what does the waiter mean by «Zusammen oder getrennt?»

To summon the bill: catch the waiter's eye and say «Die Rechnung, bitte» or «Ich möchte zahlen, bitte». «Zusammen oder getrennt?» asks whether the table pays one bill together or each person separately — a completely standard question in Germany, where splitting is normal and nobody is embarrassed by «Getrennt, bitte.» You'll then each say what you had, and the waiter totals it per person.

Tipping culture: service is included in prices, but you round up roughly 5–10% and hand it over actively — you don't leave cash on the table. Say the total you want to pay as you hand over the money: the bill is 23 €, you give 30 and say «25, bitte» (meaning: charge me 25, keep the change) or «Stimmt so» ('keep the change') if the round-up is the tip. Card payments work the same way: state the total including tip before they enter it.
What's the real difference between «sich freuen auf» and «sich freuen über»? And why did «Ich beeile mich» need the mich?

«sich freuen auf» + accusative looks forward: «Ich freue mich auf den Urlaub» (I'm looking forward to the holiday — it hasn't happened). «sich freuen über» + accusative looks at the present or past: «Ich freue mich über das Geschenk» (I'm pleased about the gift — I have it). Swapping them changes the timeline, and Germans hear the difference instantly.

«sich beeilen» is a genuinely reflexive verb: the action has no separate object, so the pronoun is structural — «Ich beeile mich», «Beeil dich!», «Wir haben uns beeilt». Some reflexives take the dative pronoun when there's already an accusative object: «Ich wasche mir die Hände» (mir = dative, die Hände = accusative) versus «Ich wasche mich» (no other object). Core everyday reflexives to learn as units: sich setzen, sich hinlegen, sich anziehen, sich entscheiden, sich erinnern an, sich interessieren für.
I need to complain about a hotel room — the heating doesn't work and it's November — without sounding aggressive. German directness scares me.

German complaints are direct about facts and softened by form, not by vagueness. At reception: «Guten Abend, ich bin in Zimmer 214. Leider funktioniert die Heizung nicht, und das Zimmer ist sehr kalt. Wäre es möglich, ein anderes Zimmer zu bekommen oder jemanden von der Haustechnik zu schicken?» The load-bearing softeners: «leider» (unfortunately — signals regret, not blame), «Wäre es möglich...» (Konjunktiv II question), and stating the problem as a fact about the room, not about a person.

If nothing happens: «Ich wäre Ihnen dankbar, wenn das heute Abend noch gelöst werden könnte.» Escalation in German works by adding deadlines and documentation, not volume: «Könnten Sie mir bitte schriftlich bestätigen, dass...?» Directness is expected and respected; what reads as rude is personal accusation («Sie haben mir ein kaltes Zimmer gegeben!»). Describe the defect, name the remedy you'd accept, keep the Sie and the Konjunktiv — that's the full recipe.
How do I say 'It's raining cats and dogs' and 'to cost an arm and a leg' in German without sounding like a phrasebook from 1970?

For heavy rain, Germans say «Es regnet in Strömen» (it's raining in streams), «Es schüttet wie aus Eimern» (it's pouring as if from buckets), or simply «Es gießt». «Katzen und Hunde» would get you a puzzled look and a look at the sky.

For expensive: «Das kostet ein Vermögen» (costs a fortune), or colloquially «Das ist sündhaft teuer» and «Das kostet eine Stange Geld». The arm-and-leg image doesn't exist. What does exist is a body idiom in the other direction: «Das geht ins Geld» (that adds up financially). A general rule for your idiom work: translate the function, then check whether German has an image of its own. Where it does — rain from buckets, money as a fortune — use theirs; where it doesn't, plain language («Das ist sehr teuer») always beats a transplanted metaphor.
Give me a polite way to give advice in German. 'You should see a doctor' / 'If I were you, I'd apologise' — my versions come out as commands.

The master key is «An deiner Stelle würde ich...» — 'In your place, I would...' — «An Ihrer Stelle würde ich mich entschuldigen.» It frames advice as your own hypothetical behaviour, which is why it lands softly. For suggestions without the frame: «Du solltest zum Arzt gehen» (solltest is Konjunktiv II of sollen — already softer than the imperative), «Es wäre besser, wenn du dich entschuldigst», or the question form «Wie wäre es, wenn du...?»

With Sie-contacts, keep everything one notch higher: «An Ihrer Stelle würde ich den Anwalt anrufen», «Vielleicht wäre es sinnvoll, ...». The blunt imperative («Geh zum Arzt!») is reserved for urgency and intimacy. Notice the system: German politeness lives in Konjunktiv II and in hypothetical framing — exactly the same machinery as polite requests, pointed in the other direction.
Why «Guten Tag» in Berlin, «Moin» in Hamburg, «Servus» in Munich, «Grüß Gott» in Passau — and which do I use where without sounding like a tourist?

Greetings are Germany's friendliest regional marker. «Moin» (from Low German 'good', not 'morning' — it's used all day) belongs to the north: Hamburg, Bremen, Schleswig-Holstein, the coast. «Servus» (Latin 'servant', i.e. 'at your service') is Bavarian and Austrian, informal-to-neutral, and doubles as goodbye. «Grüß Gott» is the polite default in Catholic Bavaria and Austria, used in shops and offices where «Guten Tag» would also be fine.

«Guten Tag» is the safe national fallback — correct everywhere, charming nowhere. The tourist tell isn't choosing wrong; it's the cheerful over-enunciation. Locals mumble their greetings («'n Tag», «Moin»), and matching the local word at low volume beats a perfect «Grüß Gott!» delivered like a stage line. In shops, add the local goodbye: north «Tschüss», Bavaria/Austria «Pfiat di» among acquaintances or «Auf Wiedersehen» formally.
Translate into natural German, keeping the register: 'Had we known about the delay, we would have taken an earlier train — but as it stands, we might as well make the best of it.'

«Hätten wir von der Verspätung gewusst, hätten wir einen früheren Zug genommen — aber so, wie es ist, machen wir am besten das Beste daraus.»

What's happening grammatically: the if-clause drops «wenn» and inverts instead — «Hätten wir... gewusst» is the formal written way to say 'if we had known', with hätte + participle marking the unreal past. The main clause mirrors it: «hätten wir... genommen». In speech you'd more likely hear «Wenn wir das gewusst hätten, hätten wir einen früheren Zug genommen.» 'Make the best of it' has a genuine German idiom: «das Beste aus etwas machen/daraus machen» — one of the happy cases where the image matches. And 'as it stands' becomes «so, wie es ist» or «bei der Lage der Dinge» in a more formal text. Don't try to import 'might as well' word for word; «am besten» carries that shrug.
My German friend texted «Hab dich nicht vergessen, melde mich morgen, versprochen!» and earlier «Der Zug hat sich verspätet, sorry». Why no ich and no articles?

German texting and diary style drops the subject pronoun in first position — a register called Tagebuchstil. «Hab dich nicht vergessen» = «Ich habe dich nicht vergessen»; «Melde mich morgen» = «Ich melde mich morgen». The verb stays in second position and the missing ich is understood. You'll see it in notes, postcards, headlines, and messages between friends.

It only works at the start of the clause and mainly with ich/wir — «Hat sich verspätet» for the train works too, since der Zug is recoverable from context. Don't use it in emails to anyone you'd address as Sie, and not in exams: it's a deliberate casual register, not carelessness. Recognising it matters more than producing it — learners often misread «Hab's verstanden» as a strange new verb form instead of a dropped subject plus «es».
What's actually different about German business letters? I have to write to a supplier: subject lines, «Betreff», the address block, and why does the date say «München, den 4. März»?

German business letters follow DIN 5008, and the conventions are visible. The subject line is labelled in older style as «Betreff:» (modern practice often omits the word and just bolds the subject) and it goes before the salutation, not after. The salutation is «Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren,» or with a name «Sehr geehrter Herr Sommer,» — and here's the famous quirk: after a comma in the salutation, the letter's first sentence continues in lowercase, because grammatically the salutation and first line form one sentence. After «Mit freundlichen Grüßen» there is no comma before your name.

The date line «München, den 4. März 2026» uses an old accusative construction ('Munich, on the 4th of March'); in the header block it's usually just «04.03.2026». Enclosures are noted as «Anlage: Vertrag (2 Seiten)» at the bottom, and «i.A.» before a signature means 'by order of' — signing on someone's behalf, a detail with legal weight in German offices.
I hear «mal», «doch», «ja», «halt» everywhere and my dictionary translations ('times', 'but', 'yes') make no sense. What are these words doing?

These are modal particles — German's tone knobs. They carry attitude, not content, and they're why word-for-word translation sounds flat. «Komm mal her» — mal softens a command into a casual request. «Das ist ja interessant!» — ja marks surprised realisation ('well, that's interesting!'). «Das habe ich dir doch gesagt» — doch insists against doubt ('I did tell you'). «Das ist halt so» — halt signals resigned acceptance ('that's just how it is').

You can delete all of them and the sentences stay grammatical — and lose their social temperature entirely. Learners should first learn to hear them (they're unstressed, mid-sentence), then adopt two: mal for softening requests and doch for friendly contradiction («Doch!» alone answers a negative question with 'yes, on the contrary' — a word English doesn't have). Overusing particles as a learner sounds theatrical; underusing them sounds robotic. Aim for mal and doch and let the rest arrive by exposure.
Sort out «kennen», «wissen», and «kennenlernen» for me. I said «Ich kenne die Antwort» and «Ich weiß Maria seit Jahren».

Both sentences swap the verbs. «wissen» is for facts and information: «Ich weiß die Antwort», «Weißt du, wann der Zug fährt?» — it takes a clause or a fact-noun. «kennen» is for familiarity with people, places, and things: «Ich kenne Maria seit Jahren», «Kennst du Berlin?» — it takes a person/place/object, never a clause. Your second sentence needed kennen precisely because Maria is a person and «seit Jahren» measures acquaintance.

«kennenlernen» is the event of first meeting: «Wir haben uns in Wien kennengelernt» — note it's a separable verb and describes the beginning, not the state. English 'know' covers all three territories, which is why this trio traps every learner. A fourth neighbour: «können» (to be able / to know a skill or language) — «Sie kann gut Deutsch» uses können, not kennen. Test yourself: fact → wissen, person/place → kennen, first meeting → kennenlernen, skill → können.
I'm staying with a host family in Freiburg. What do I say at the table — asking to pass things, complimenting the food, declining seconds politely?

The working phrases: «Könntest du mir bitte das Salz reichen?» (reichen = to pass/hand). «Es schmeckt wirklich lecker» or stronger «Das schmeckt ausgezeichnet» — compliments on food are expected and warmly received; about the cook's signature dish, ask «Ist das ein Familienrezept?» and you'll get a story with it. Before eating, the host may say «Guten Appetit» — answer «Danke, gleichfalls» ('likewise').

Declining seconds: «Nein danke, ich bin satt» — careful: «Ich bin voll» is understandable but coarse at a family table (it suggests stuffed/drunk); «satt» is the polite word for having eaten enough. If you must leave food, apologise lightly: «Es tut mir leid, ich schaffe es einfach nicht mehr — es war aber sehr lecker.» And a small cultural note: in many German homes you wait until the host begins or says «Guten Appetit» before starting, and keeping hands (not elbows) visible on the table is old-fashioned good manners that grandparents still notice.
«Ich interessiere mich für Musik», «Ich erinnere mich an den Tag», «Ich freue mich auf morgen» — why do reflexive verbs each demand a different preposition?

Because in German the preposition belongs to the verb as part of its government, and there's no master rule — but there are patterns worth memorising with the verb as one chunk: sich interessieren für (+Akk), sich erinnern an (+Akk), sich freuen auf (+Akk, future) / über (+Akk, present), sich bewerben um (+Akk, a job), sich kümmern um (+Akk), sich beschweren bei (person, Dat) über (thing, Akk), sich gewöhnen an (+Akk).

The good news: the case after these prepositions is almost always accusative, so the real learning load is just which preposition. Dictionaries mark it as «sich erinnern an (+Akk)» — treat that whole string as the vocabulary item. English speakers stumble because English varies its prepositions too ('interested in', 'remind of'), but German exams and employers notice these; they're a shibboleth of advanced competence. Learn the top twenty reflexive verbs with their prepositions and you'll cover nearly all daily use.
What's the difference between «am Montag», «montags», «jeden Montag», and «nächsten Montag»? My course meets weekly and I keep tangling them.

Four different meanings. «am Montag» = on Monday (one specific Monday, usually the nearest). «montags» (lowercase, with -s) = on Mondays, habitually: «Montags habe ich Deutschkurs» — that's your weekly course. «jeden Montag» = every Monday, explicit and complete: «Der Kurs findet jeden Montag statt.» «nächsten Montag» = next Monday (the one coming in the following week for many speakers; the nearest Monday for others — Germans genuinely argue about this one, so add the date when it matters).

Same system for parts of day: «am Morgen» (specific), «morgens» (habitually), «heute Morgen» (this morning — no preposition), «in der Nacht» but «nachts». And seasons/dates: «im Sommer», «am 3. Mai», «im Jahr 2026» — but «2026» alone in speech is often just «zweitausendsechsundzwanzig». Habitual adverbials with -s (abends, mittags, werktags) are the ones learners underuse most.
Teach me the phone call to a landlord about a broken heater. It's October, the flat is cold, I'm a tenant not a friend.

Register: polite Sie, factual, with a clear request. «Guten Tag, hier spricht Anna Roth, Ihre Mieterin aus der Lindenstraße 12, zweiter Stock. Ich rufe an, weil die Heizung seit gestern nicht funktioniert. Die Heizkörper bleiben kalt, auch auf Stufe fünf.» Then the request in Konjunktiv II: «Könnten Sie bitte einen Handwerker schicken? Ich bin heute und morgen den ganzen Tag zu Hause.»

Useful vocabulary: der Heizkörper (radiator), die Stufe (setting level), der Handwerker (tradesperson), der Hausmeister (caretaker — often your first call instead of the landlord), die Nebenkostenabrechnung (annual service-charge statement). If nothing happens, the written follow-up starts «Sehr geehrter Herr Berger, bezugnehmend auf unser Telefonat vom...» — German tenancy runs on documented paper trails, and a calm, dated letter is a stronger tool than a second, louder call.
Why does German write «des Kindes», «des Mannes», «des Tages» but «der Frau», «der Kinder»? And when do I use «dessen» vs «wessen»?

The genitive marks masculine and neuter nouns with -(e)s: des Kindes, des Mannes, des Tages (long stems prefer -es: des Jahres; short stems often -s: des Monats is standard despite being short — usage settles these). Feminine and plural nouns show genitive only on the article: der Frau, der Kinder — the noun itself stays bare, which is why «wegen Kinder» errors happen: the article must carry the case.

«dessen» (masculine/neuter) and «deren» (feminine/plural) are the genitive relative and demonstrative pronouns: «der Mann, dessen Auto gestohlen wurde», «die Frau, deren Bruder ich kenne». «wessen» is the question word: «Wessen Buch ist das?» — 'Whose book is that?' Don't confuse «dessen» with «das» in speech rhythm; in formal writing dessen/deren are preferred over the colloquial «dem sein» constructions you'll hear in dialect («dem Mann sein Auto») — charming in a Bavarian kitchen, wrong in a contract.
I keep reading «z.B.», «bzw.», «usw.», «ca.», «d.h.» in German emails. Decode the abbreviation system.

The core set: «z.B.» = zum Beispiel (for example). «usw.» = und so weiter (etc.). «d.h.» = das heißt (that is, i.e.). «ca.» = circa (approximately). «bzw.» = beziehungsweise — the trickiest: it means 'or rather / respectively / and/or', specifying a relationship: «der Lehrer bzw. die Lehrerin» (the teacher, or rather the female teacher), «Montag bzw. Dienstag» (Monday or Tuesday respectively, depending).

More office staples: «ggf.» = gegebenenfalls (if applicable), «i.d.R.» = in der Regel (as a rule), «u.a.» = unter anderem (among other things), «v.a.» = vor allem (above all), «s.o.» = siehe oben (see above), «Abb.» = Abbildung (figure). Notice German abbreviations keep their periods and are read aloud as full words. «bzw.» has no single English equivalent — translate it by deciding which relation it marks in that sentence, not by reaching for a fixed word.
Explain «doch» as an answer. Someone asked «Du kommst nicht mit?» and my friend just said «Doch!» — one word, whole argument.

German has a three-way answer system where English has two. «Ja» confirms a positive question («Kommst du mit?» — «Ja»). «Nein» confirms a negative one («Du kommst nicht mit?» — «Nein» = correct, I'm not coming). «Doch» contradicts a negative question or statement: «Du kommst nicht mit?» — «Doch!» = on the contrary, I AM coming.

It's one of the highest-value single words in the language because English forces a full clause ('Yes, I am!') where German fires one syllable. The same doch works as a particle inside sentences to push back against an assumption: «Das habe ich doch gesagt!» ('I did say that!'). Learners from English often answer negative questions with «Ja» meaning 'yes, I'm coming' — which Germans hear as confirmation that you're not. When the question contains nicht or kein, pause and choose between nein (agreeing with the negative) and doch (rejecting it).
How do I read German numbers in the wild — prices, years, phone numbers? «1,99 €», «1999», «0176...» all seem to follow different rules.

Three separate conventions. Prices use a decimal comma: 1,99 € is read «ein Euro neunundneunzig» — and the comma means the dot is the thousands separator, so 1.999 € is nearly two thousand euros, not two. Years are read as hundreds before 2000: 1999 = «neunzehnhundertneunundneunzig»; from 2000 on, «zweitausendneun» for 2009, «zweitausendsechsundzwanzig» for 2026.

Phone numbers are dictated in pairs or singly, never in English-style triplets: 0176 2345 6789 comes out as «null eins sieben sechs, dreiundzwanzig fünfundvierzig...» — pairs read as two-digit numbers. And the number order inside German compounds runs ones-before-tens: 24 is «vierundzwanzig» ('four-and-twenty'), which is why beginners mishear 24 as 42 under pressure. Practice by reading prices aloud in supermarkets; it's the fastest drill there is.
Why do Germans say «Wir sind Papst» and «Schland»? And what is «die Mannschaft»? I'm trying to follow football talk at work.

These are media-made phrases. «Wir sind Papst!» ('We are Pope!') was the Bild newspaper's headline in 2005 when Joseph Ratzinger became Benedict XVI — still quoted jokingly whenever a German achieves something big. «Schland» is the chant-compressed form of Deutschland from the 2006 home World Cup, the summer public viewing and flag-waving became normal in Germany.

«Die Mannschaft» — literally 'the team' — was the official brand name of the national team from 2015; the federation retired it in 2022 after fans found it corporate, so you'll now hear it used ironically or by older fans. Other pub-talk essentials: «der Ball ist rund» (the ball is round — anything can happen), «das Runde muss ins Eckige» (the round thing must go in the rectangular thing — score a goal), and «Abseits» (offside). Football small talk is a genuine integration skill in German offices; Monday-morning match talk is the «Wie war dein Wochenende» of the sports page.
My teacher marked «Ich habe ihn gesehen gehabt» wrong but Germans say things like «Ich hatte das schon gemacht gehabt». What's the double perfect and should I use it?

The double perfect («gesehen gehabt», «gemacht gehabt») is real colloquial German, especially in the south and in spoken narration: it adds a layer of 'already done and dusted' beyond the pluperfect. «Ich hatte das schon gemacht gehabt» ≈ 'I had already gotten that done (by then, and it was settled)'. Your teacher marked it wrong because in standard written German it's not accepted — exams, essays, and formal prose want the simple pluperfect: «Ich hatte ihn gesehen.»

Treat it as recognition-only vocabulary, like the double infinitive's spoken cousins. The same advice applies to «am Arbeiten sein» (the Rhineland progressive: «Ich bin am Schreiben» = I'm in the middle of writing) — spreading in speech, charming, and still marked wrong in a Goethe-Institut exam. Standard German has no progressive; the present tense plus context does the job. Knowing which forms are dialect-colloquial versus standard is itself an advanced skill — your ear is ahead of your pen, which is the right order.
I'm working a holiday job at a Tokyo department store. What exactly do I say when a customer enters, when they ask where something is, and when they leave with a purchase?

The three anchor phrases: on entry, 「いらっしゃいませ」 — never answered, it's a welcome call, delivered brightly. When asked for help, respond 「かしこまりました」 (certainly, understood — politer than 「分かりました」) and when you need them to wait: 「少々お待ちくださいませ」. If you must go and check stock: 「ただいま確認してまいります」 — まいります is the humble form of 行く/来る, because the action is yours.

At the register: 「お買い上げありがとうございます」 as you hand over the bag with both hands, and if they're leaving empty-handed, still 「ありがとうございました。またお越しくださいませ」. Notice the past tense ありがとうございました for completed service — ありがとうございます is for something ongoing or about to happen. Staff Japanese (接客敬語) is a fixed script more than a grammar exercise; learning the twenty standard lines verbatim will carry you through most shifts.
A client phoned and asked for my boss, Tanaka. I said «田中さんは今いません» and my Japanese coworker winced. What's the correct way to say the boss is out?

The wince is about uchi/soto (inside/outside). To a client, your boss is 'inside' — so you strip his title and use humble language about him, exactly as you would about yourself: 「田中はただいま席を外しております」 (Tanaka is away from his desk at the moment). No さん, no 部長, and おります (humble いる) instead of います. The client, by contrast, gets full honorifics: 「いつもお世話になっております」.

The logic shocks learners — surely the boss deserves respect? He does, but in Japanese business etiquette you lower your whole in-group before an out-group member; elevating your boss to a client would be like boasting about your own family. If the client asks when he'll return: 「三時ごろ戻る予定でございます」. And never say «田中様» about your own boss to an outsider — that's the mirror-image error.
Give me the honorific (尊敬語) verb set I actually need: 言う、見る、食べる、来る、いる、する、知っている — and how to spot the pattern.

The core irregulars, which cover most of daily business: 言う → おっしゃる; 見る → ご覧になる; 食べる・飲む → 召し上がる; 来る・行く・いる → いらっしゃる (one form covers all three); する → なさる; 知っている → ご存じです. Examples: 「社長がおっしゃいました」 (the president said), 「資料をご覧ください」 (please look at the documents), 「部長は会議室にいらっしゃいます」.

For verbs without a special form, use the productive pattern お/ご + verb stem + になる: 読む → お読みになる, 書く → お書きになる, 会議する → ご出席になる... (careful: 出席する takes ご because it's a Sino-Japanese compound). The passive form can also do honorific duty (先生が書かれた本), which is why you'll hear it — but the special forms sound more polished. Pair this with the humble set (申す、拝見する、参る、うかがう、いたす) and you have the two directions of the whole system: raise them, lower yourself.
Now the humble side (謙譲語): how do I say 'I will go to your office tomorrow', 'I read your report', and 'My name is...' in proper business Japanese?

Three models. Going: 「明日、御社の事務所にうかがいます」 — うかがう is the humble verb for visiting (and also for asking). Reading: 「報告書を拝見しました」 — 拝見する is humble 見る, used for things received from or belonging to the other party. Introducing: 「田中と申します」 — 申す is humble 言う; on the phone it's 「株式会社サクラの田中と申します」.

The productive humble pattern is お/ご + stem + する: 「ご案内します」 (I'll show you around), 「お持ちします」 (I'll bring it), 「ご連絡いたします」 (I'll contact you — いたす is humble する). Two cautions: humble forms describe YOUR actions toward the respected person — never use 拝見する for something unrelated to them. And 申します is for names and statements you make; don't stack it into every sentence, or you slide into over-politeness that native speakers hear as stiffness.
When do nouns take お and when ご? お電話、ご意見、お茶、ご家族 — is there a rule or is it pure memorisation?

There's a working rule: native Japanese (kun-reading) words take お — お茶、お金、お名前、お手紙. Sino-Japanese (on-reading, usually two-kanji compounds) take ご — ご意見、ご家族、ご連絡、ご住所. 電話 is a compound but takes お電話 in set service phrases, which is why it confused you — it's an entrenched exception, as is お返事 (a compound that takes お).

Loanwords from English take neither: you don't say おコーヒー in polite standard speech (though おビール is heard jokingly and in some casual service talk). A few words never take a prefix because they're already humble or because the combination sounds wrong — ✕お死ぬ. And some prefixes beautify rather than honour (お弁当、お祭り — the speaker isn't respecting the lunchbox). Rule of use: prefix the other person's belongings and actions （お名前、ご住所）, not your own — except set phrases like お手紙を書きます where usage is fixed.
My textbook-loving colleague says «おっしゃられていらっしゃいました» and «ご覧になられました». My native boss quietly corrected him. What error is this?

二重敬語 — double keigo: stacking two honorific devices on one verb. おっしゃる is already the honorific of 言う； adding the honorific-passive 〜られる makes おっしゃられる, which is nonstandard. Likewise ご覧になる already honours 見る, so ご覧になられる doubles it. The correct forms are simply 「おっしゃっていました」 and 「ご覧になりました」.

The trap is understandable: 〜れる/られる can mark respect, so learners insure themselves twice. A few double forms are so widespread they've been officially accepted as fixed — お召し上がりになる is the famous one (the Agency for Cultural Affairs tolerates it). But as a learner, treat one honorific device per verb as the law. Related over-politeness to avoid: applying honorifics to your own actions （私がご覧になりました ✕ → 拝見しました) and させていただく inflation — 「ご説明させていただきます» is fine, but using it for things needing no permission («休ませていただきます» for your own day off, announced to no one) is a modern pet peeve of native speakers.
At a Japanese office I need to answer the phone. Walk me through the first twenty seconds when the caller asks for someone.

Pick up by the third ring: 「お電話ありがとうございます。株式会社ハルの山田でございます。」 (Thank you for calling. This is Yamada of Haru Co.) If you were slow: 「お待たせいたしました」 first. The caller names themselves; respond 「いつもお世話になっております」 — the universal business lubricant, roughly 'thank you for your continued support'.

If they ask for a colleague: 「佐藤ですね。ただいまおつなぎいたしますので、少々お待ちくださいませ。」 Then the hold music. If the person is out, you switch to the uchi/soto script: 「佐藤はただいま外出しております」 and offer 「戻りましたら、こちらからお電話いたしましょうか」 (shall I have her call you back?). Closing, once the business is done: 「それでは、失礼いたします」 — and wait a beat before hanging up; in Japanese phone etiquette the caller (or the junior party) hangs up last, and slamming the receiver first is a real, noticed rudeness.
The convenience store clerk asked «温めますか» and later said «お弁当になります». My teacher says one of these is wrong Japanese. Which, and why do clerks say it?

「温めますか」 (Shall I heat it up?) is perfectly fine. The suspect is 「お弁当になります» — literally 'it becomes a bento'. なる means 'become', and the bento isn't becoming anything; the clerk means 'here is your bento'. Correct service Japanese would be 「こちら、お弁当でございます」. This 〜になります pattern is the famous example of コンビニ敬語 (also called マニュアル敬語): chains train staff from manuals, and the forms spread because they sound vaguely soft and polite.

Other specimens you'll hear daily: 「千円からお預かりします» (から is odd — it should be 千円お預かりします; they're holding your 1,000 yen note while making change) and 「〜のほう» padding («レシートのほうは...»). None of this will block communication, and you should never correct a clerk — but don't copy these into a job interview or business email, where they're recognised as errors. Understanding them is part of listening fluency in modern Japan.
I'm emailing a Japanese professor to ask about joining her lab. Give me the skeleton: subject line, opening, the request itself, closing.

Subject: 「研究室訪問のお願い（学部3年・佐藤）」— state purpose and who you are. Opening: 「突然のご連絡失礼いたします。〇〇大学経済学部3年の佐藤健と申します。」(Forgive the out-of-the-blue contact; I'm Ken Sato, third-year, economics.) Professors are addressed as 先生, and inside the mail you refer to her with honorifics: 「先生のご研究に大変興味を持ち、ご連絡いたしました。」

The request, softened with humble forms and a cushion: 「可能であれば、一度研究室を訪問し、お話をうかがうことは可能でしょうか。」 Close with 「ご多忙のところ恐縮ですが、ご検討いただけますと幸いです。何卒よろしくお願い申し上げます。」Two practical notes: don't open with 拝啓 in email (that's for paper letters; if you do use it, it must pair with 敬具 at the end). And never write お疲れ様です to a professor — that's for colleagues inside a workplace, not for teachers.
「私は学生です» vs «私が学生です» — my teacher says both are correct but mean different things. English only has one 'I am a student'.

The difference is what the sentence is about. 「私は学生です» presents 私 as the topic — 'As for me, (I'm) a student' — the natural answer to 'Tell me about yourself'. 「私が学生です» marks 私 with が, which singles it out: this answers 'Who here is a student?' — 'I'm the one who is a student', with an exhaustive flavour: me, not the others.

The classic classroom demo: «誰が来ますか» (Who's coming?) must be answered 「田中さんが来ます», never 田中さんは — the question word and its answer both take が, because が marks the new, selected information, while は marks the established topic the sentence comments on. Swap them and you sound like you're changing the subject. A useful first approximation: は = 'as for X' (you already know we're talking about X), が = 'it's X (who/that...)' (X is the news). It takes years to fully master, but the question-answer test — が answers question words — will rescue most of your sentences.
Why is it «図書館で勉強する» but «図書館にいる», and «公園で子供が遊んでいる» but «公園に子供がいる»? The で/に location split confuses me.

The rule: で marks the location where an action takes place; に marks the location where something or someone exists (with いる/ある). Studying is an action → 「図書館で勉強する». Existing is not → 「図書館にいる». Your park pair shows both halves: children playing is an activity （で遊んでいる), children being there is existence （にいる).

Test with the verb: if you can add an object and an activity (read a book, eat lunch, hold a meeting), use で: 「会議室で会議をする». If the sentence is just 'X is in Y', use に: 「会議室に机がある». Events flip learners most: concerts and parties are actions that 'take place', so 「ホールでコンサートがある» — ある with events takes で, because the event happens there rather than merely existing. Destination に («学校に行く») is a third job of に, marking where movement ends.
«学校に行く» and «学校へ行く» — same meaning? And why did my host mother correct «買い物へ行く» differently from «映画を見に行く»?

行く with に and へ are nearly interchangeable for destination; へ (read え) leans slightly toward direction — the path rather than the arrival point — and sounds a touch more literary. In daily speech に dominates. Where they split: only に works for purpose — 「映画を見に行く» (go to see a film), 「買い物に行く» (go shopping). へ cannot do purpose: ✕見へ行く is impossible.

Your host mother's correction was probably about that purpose pattern: the shape is verb-stem + に + movement verb （食べに行く、迎えに来る、遊びに来る). One more contrast: に marks a precise target including time points （三時に、月曜日に), while へ never marks time. So the working rule: default to に everywhere; use へ when you want a directional, slightly written flavour — and never for purpose or time.
Why «月曜日に会いましょう» but just «明日会いましょう» with no に? And is «来週に» wrong?

に attaches to absolute, calendar-anchored time points: days of the week, dates, clock times, months, years — 「月曜日に», 「三時に», 「五月に», 「2027年に». Relative time words — 明日、今日、昨日、今朝、今晩、来週、来月、来年 — point from 'now' rather than sitting on the calendar grid, and they take no に. So yes, «来週に» is a classic learner error; just say 「来週会いましょう».

Border cases: seasons usually take no に （春休みます is odd; 春に休みます is fine when you mean 'in spring' as a specific slot — usage varies, with に optional). 朝 and 夜 alone take no に （朝起きます), but a specific clock-qualified morning does: 「朝の七時に». Memory hook: if you can circle it on a calendar or clock, に; if it's defined relative to today, no に.
«水を飲みたい» or «水が飲みたい»? And why «日本語が分かる» and «ピアノが弾ける» instead of を?

Both water sentences exist, with a nuance: 「水が飲みたい» treats the desire as a state focused on the water — the standard textbook form, because たい behaves like an adjective, and adjectives take が for their target. 「水を飲みたい» is also heard and accepted; を highlights the action of drinking. With たい, exams prefer が.

分かる, できる, and the potential forms （弾ける、読める) belong to the same family: they describe states and abilities, not deliberate actions, so their objects take が: 「日本語が分かります», 「ピアノが弾けます», 「納豆が食べられます» (can eat natto — ability). The pattern to internalise: 好き、嫌い、上手、下手、欲しい、分かる、できる、potential forms, たい — all が. Plain action verbs keep を: 「ピアノを弾きます» (I play the piano — the activity) vs 「ピアノが弾けます» (I can play — the ability). That activity/ability contrast is the deepest version of the rule.
What is は doing in «ビールは飲みますが、ワインは飲みません» that が couldn't do?

This is は's second job: contrast. 「ビールは飲みますが、ワインは飲みません» means 'Beer, I drink; wine, I don't' — each は lifts its noun up for comparison, implying a set (alcoholic drinks) within which you're sorting. が couldn't do this job; 「ビールが飲みます» is ungrammatical because 飲みます needs a topic here, and が would try to make beer the selected subject of drinking.

Contrastive は also hides inside negatives: 「日本語は話せません» often means 'Japanese, at least, I can't speak (implying other languages may differ)', and 「ご飯は食べました» can imply 'the rice I ate (but maybe not the rest)'. This is why は appears where beginners expect が after objects and time words: the speaker is comparing, not just stating. When you hear a slightly stressed は mid-sentence, ask 'compared to what?' — there's always an implied other item.
Counters are breaking me. How do I order three beers, two coffees, buy four tickets and five stamps — all different counters?

Welcome to the counter system — the counter follows the shape or category of the thing. Beer in bottles or glasses: 本 (long cylindrical objects) — 「ビール三本» (さんぼん; note the sound change). Coffee in cups: 杯 — 「コーヒー二杯» (にはい). Tickets: 枚 (flat things) — 「切符四枚». Stamps are also flat: 「切手五枚». At a restaurant the order shape is noun + number + counter + をください: 「ビール三本と、切符…» — well, tickets elsewhere.

Sound changes to drill: 本 goes ぽん/ぼん after certain numbers （一本 いっぽん、三本 さんぼん); 杯 goes ぱい （一杯 いっぱい、三杯 さんばい); 匹 for animals does the same （一匹 いっぴき). When you don't know the counter, the native fallback is the generic つ system （一つ、二つ…) for up to about ten, or 個 for small objects — nobody will misunderstand 「ビール三つください» in a loud izakaya, but 三本 is the mark of someone who's learning properly.
Why is one person 一人 (ひとり) and two people 二人 (ふたり) but three people 三人 (さんにん)? And how do I ask 'how many people?'

人 (にん) is the counter for people, but the first two counts keep ancient native Japanese readings: 一人 ひとり, 二人 ふたり. From three on it's regular Sino-Japanese + にん: 三人 さんにん、四人 よにん (not しにん — し is avoided, as it sounds like death), 七人 しちにん/ななにん、八人 はちにん. 'How many people?' is 「何人ですか» — なんにん.

In the wild: a restaurant host will ask 「何名様ですか» — 名 (めい) is the polite customer-counter, and 様 does the honouring. Answer 「二人です» or 「三名です» both work; staff register uses 名. Watch also 四人 at hotels: よにん. The ひとり/ふたり pair shows up elsewhere too — 一人で (alone, by oneself) is a set phrase you'll use constantly: 「一人で東京へ行きました».
My neighbour has two cats, a big dog, and three goldfish. Which counters — and why did the pet shop use a different one for the horse in a photo?

Small animals take 匹 （ひき): 「猫二匹» (にひき), 「金魚三匹» (さんびき) — and the dog, if it's a normal pet dog, also 匹： 「犬一匹». The horse takes 頭 （とう), the counter for large animals — cattle, horses, elephants: 「馬一頭». The size line is roughly 'could a person carry it': carryable → 匹， not carryable → 頭. That's why a huge dog is still 一匹 (you could, in principle, lift it) while a pony is 一頭.

Birds and rabbits take 羽 （わ): 「鳥二羽». Fish sold as food may be 尾 （び) at a fishmonger's. Insects are 匹. The counter system encodes a folk taxonomy — medium creatures you hold, big livestock, winged things — and native speakers choose instantly. For pets there's an emotional wrinkle: some owners count a beloved dog with 頭 to make it sound grander, and pet obituaries often use 頭. When unsure for animals: 匹 for anything pet-sized, 頭 for farm-sized, 羽 if it has wings.
How do particles stack? I saw «東京には», «教室では», «友達とだけ», and «へは». What's the logic of the order?

Japanese particles layer in a fixed order: case particles （が、を) come first in the stack conceptually, then は/も/だけ/しか can attach after other particles. So 「東京には住みたくない» = 東京に + は (contrastive topic: 'Tokyo, at least, I don't want to live in'), 「教室では静かにしてください» = 教室で + は. With へ: 「彼へは連絡しました» (to him, I did contact — contrast implied).

Key asymmetries: は and も replace が and を entirely （私は, 水も — you never say がは or をは), but they stack after に、で、へ、と、から、まで: 「友達とだけ話す» (talk only with friends), 「日本からも来ました». だけ can also precede: 「だけは» reverses the emphasis — 「それだけはできません» (that alone I cannot do). Learn it as: が/を are fragile and get displaced; the relational particles are sturdy and take は/も/だけ on top.
ね、よ、よね — my Japanese friends end every sentence with these and I can't tell what changes. Also, is it OK at work?

They manage shared knowledge. よ pushes new information at the listener: 「雨が降っていますよ» — 'It's raining (I'm telling you)'. ね seeks agreement or softens: 「いい天気ですね» — 'Nice weather, isn't it'. よね does both: 「明日は休みですよね» — 'Tomorrow's a day off, right? (I'm fairly sure and checking)'. Choosing wrong flips the social meaning: announcing something the listener knows better than you with よ can sound pushy; ね on a hard fact can sound unsure.

At work with です/ます style, ね and よね are completely normal and soften business speech: 「三時から会議ですね». よ after です is fine too but firmer — managers use it downward more than staff use it upward. In keigo-heavy settings (to clients), sentence-final particles thin out; internal chat with colleagues is where they bloom. One warning: in plain-form speech, よ and ね also carry gendered stereotypes in textbooks that real speakers follow much more loosely today — listen to your actual friends, not the stereotype.
あげる、くれる、もらう — I gave flowers to my teacher and said «先生に花をくれました». Everyone laughed. Fix my mental model.

The model is a camera position: giving verbs point toward or away from your in-group. あげる: giving away from you to someone else — 「私が友達に花をあげました». くれる: giving toward you or your in-group — 「友達が私に花をくれました» — the giver is the subject, and the receiver is you/your side. Your sentence made the teacher the giver and you the receiver — the exact reverse of what happened; correct is 「先生に花をあげました».

もらう flips perspective to the receiver: 「私は先生に教えてもらいました» — 'I received teaching from the teacher', with the giver marked by に. With superiors, あげる is often upgraded to 差し上げる, くれる to くださる, もらう to いただく: 「先生が本をくださいました», 「本をいただきました». The laughter wasn't cruelty — reversed giving verbs are the single most reliable learner tell in Japanese, because English 'give' has no direction built in. Anchor: くれる always lands on your side of the fence.
What do てあげる、てくれる、てもらう add? Why is «窓を開けてあげました» sometimes kind and sometimes arrogant?

Attached to the て-form, the giving verbs mark who benefits from an action. てくれる: someone did something for your benefit — 「友達が駅まで送ってくれました» (my friend kindly drove me to the station). てもらう: you received the favour — 「友達に送ってもらいました». Same event, two camera angles, and てくれる is the warmer, more grateful framing. てあげる: you did it for someone — 「弟に本を読んであげました».

The arrogance trap: てあげる announces your own generosity, so to equals or superiors it can sound like you're keeping score — telling your boss «資料を作ってあげました» is a career error. With children, pets, plants, and close juniors it's natural and kind. Toward superiors, Japanese often drops the benefit marker entirely or uses humble させていただく constructions. Rule of thumb: advertise favours received （てくれる/てもらう), stay quiet about favours given — let the other person say てくれた about you.
How do I say 'I feed the dog' and 'I water the plants'? A textbook told me not to use あげる there.

The textbook means やる: for recipients ranked clearly below you — animals, plants, small children in casual speech — やる is the traditional giving verb: 「犬に餌をやる», 「花に水をやる». あげる was historically considered too elevated for animals; the logic is the same hierarchy that made やる the plain 'give' for downward directions.

Modern usage is softening: many pet owners say 「犬に餌をあげる» because the pet is family, and あげる to children is now standard in polite speech. やる survives strongly with plants （水をやる is nearly fixed) and in rough masculine speech between friends («貸してやる»). What you must not do is やる toward a person of equal or higher standing — 「先生にやりました» would be genuinely rude. This is the giving system encoding social height in a single verb choice; plants get やる, teachers get 差し上げる, and your dog lives in the negotiable middle.

At the office a client gave us sweets. My coworker said «いただきます» before eating one at her desk, and later told the client «ありがとうございました» — but for the gift itself she said something with いただく. Sort this out.

いただく does three jobs. First, it's the humble verb for receiving: 「お菓子をいただきました» — 'we received the sweets' (lowering yourself before the giver). Telling the client this — or 「美味しくいただきました» (we ate them with pleasure) — reports the gift's happy fate, which is exactly what givers want to hear. Second, いただきます before eating is the same word fossilised as a ritual: 'I humbly receive this food', said to the room, the cook, the universe — hence your coworker at her desk.

Third, in てもらう's polite form: 「ご説明いただきました» (we received your explanation). The pattern: whenever the receiver is you/your side and the giver deserves respect, もらう upgrades to いただく and あげる from them upgrades to くださる. Gifts in Japanese offices are also acknowledged later — a small return gift （お返し) or a thank-you message the next day keeps the ledger balanced; silence after receiving is the actual faux pas, not any single verb.
Decode these station signs for me: 各駅停車、快速、特急、自由席、指定席、4番線. I'm tired of boarding the wrong trains.

These six will fix your railway life. 各駅停車 （かくえきていしゃ) = local, stops at every station. 快速 （かいそく) = rapid, skips smaller stations — no extra fare on JR. 特急 （とっきゅう) = limited express, fastest and fewest stops, and it needs a special express ticket on top of the base fare. 自由席 = unreserved seating (first come, first served); 指定席 = reserved seat with an assigned car and seat number. 番線 is the platform/track: 「4番線» is platform 4 — announcements say 「4番線に電車がまいります».

Two more that pair with these: 急行 (express — between 快速 and 特急 in stopping pattern on private lines, terminology varies by company) and 準急 (semi-express). And the trap word: 普通 can mean 'normal' but on departure boards it labels the local train （普通列車). Before boarding, match three things: train type colour on the board, destination, and whether your ticket covers the 特急 surcharge. The signs are consistent nationwide once you can read them.
I have to fill in a form at city hall. What are these fields: 氏名、フリガナ、住所、生年月日、電話番号、世帯主、印鑑?

The standard 住民票-world form vocabulary: 氏名 = full name (surname + given name, usually with surname first in its own box). フリガナ = the phonetic reading of your name in katakana, written above the kanji — for a foreign name, write your name in katakana as it appears on your residence card. 住所 = address, written from largest to smallest: prefecture, city, district, block, building, room. 生年月日 = date of birth — often with era years （令和・平成・昭和） to circle; your My Number or residence documents use the Western year too.

電話番号 = phone number. 世帯主 = head of household — for a single-person household, that's you. 印鑑 is the personal seal (hanko) you stamp instead of signing; many forms now accept サイン for foreign residents, but some still require a registered seal （実印） for major contracts, versus the everyday 認印. Bring your residence card, and copy your name and address exactly as printed on it — mismatches between form and card are the number-one cause of a second trip to city hall.
When can I drop です/ます? My diary is in plain form, my coworker chat is plain, but my section chief gets です/ます. Where are the actual lines?

Plain form is the language of intimacy, interiority, and downward address. Diary and notes to yourself: plain, always — です in a diary reads like writing a report on yourself. Friends, family, and close coworkers of similar age after the relationship warms: plain, with sentence-final particles doing the friendliness work. Your section chief: です/ます (丁寧語) is the floor, not the ceiling — it's the neutral-professional default for anyone senior, any client, any stranger, and any formal setting regardless of who's listening.

The subtle part is switching: many workplaces run on です/ます during meetings and plain form at the after-work drink, and the switch itself signals 'we're off duty now'. Mixed style — です/ます sentences with plain subordinate clauses («行くと思います», «安いけど») — is normal, because subordinate clauses are always plain even in polite speech. What reads as rude isn't plain form itself but plain form aimed upward without a relationship to support it. When in doubt, start です/ます and let the senior person set the temperature.
Why must it be «明日は雨だと思います» and «忙しいから行けません» — why do the clauses before と思う and から have to be plain even in polite speech?

Because Japanese politeness is marked once, at the end of the sentence, and subordinate clauses stay in plain form underneath it. と思います quotes your thought: the quoted content keeps its natural plain shape — 「雨だと思います», 「彼は来ないと思います». Writing 「雨ですと思います» is a classic error; the です belongs only to the main verb 思います. Same with から/けど/ので: 「忙しいから行けません», «高いけど買います» — the reason clause is plain, the conclusion carries the politeness.

Exceptions that prove the architecture: quoted speech preserves the original style （彼は「行きます」と言いました — the quote keeps its ます because that's what he said), and formal writing sometimes levels everything up. But the everyday rule is strict: one politeness marker per sentence, at the end. This is also why plain forms matter even if you only ever speak politely — half of every polite sentence is built from them.
