Loanword traps: my landlord called my apartment a マンション, my friend does アルバイト at a café, and a shop sign said スマートなデザイン. None of these mean what I expected.

Three famous false friends. マンション is not a mansion — it's a mid-to-high-rise concrete apartment building (often nicer than an アパート, which is a small wooden block). アルバイト is a part-time job, borrowed from German Arbeit via students in the Meiji era — your friend isn't 'working' in general, she's a part-timer; the verb is アルバイトをする or バイトする. スマート describes a slim, stylish silhouette — スマートな人 is slender and well-dressed, not clever (clever is 頭がいい/賢い).

More of the family: カンニング = cheating on an exam (from 'cunning' — the dishonest sense only). テンションが高い = excited, in high spirits — the opposite of English 'tension'. サービス at a shop often means free of charge / on the house （サービスです = it's complimentary). コンセント is an electrical outlet — from 'concentric plug', a century-old coinage. Gairaigo are Japanese words now; always check the local meaning rather than trusting the English echo.
How do time counters work? I need 'three hours', 'two weeks', 'half past four', and 'a five-minute walk' for real sentences.

Durations take dedicated counters. Hours: 時間 — 「三時間勉強しました» (for three hours). Clock points use 時 without 間: 「四時半に会いましょう» — 半 (はん) is 'half past', so 四時半 is 4:30. Minutes: 分 (ふん/ぷん with sound changes) — 「駅まで徒歩五分です» (five minutes on foot), 「十分待ってください» (じっぷん, ten minutes). Weeks: 週間 — 「二週間旅行しました»; 'last week/next week' are 先週/来週, not counter phrases.

The 間 is the trap: it marks duration span. 三時 is a moment (3 o'clock), 三時間 is a length (three hours). Drop 間 and your 'I studied for three hours' becomes 'I studied at three o'clock'. Days behave similarly: 一日 can be the 1st of the month or a one-day duration; 二日間 makes the duration explicit. And 半 works for durations too: 「一時間半» — an hour and a half, the single most useful time phrase in travel Japanese.
りんごを一つ、卵を10個、ケーキをホールで一つ — when do I use the 一つ・二つ system and when 個?

The 一つ (ひとつ) system is the native generic counter: 一つ、二つ、三つ、四つ、五つ、六つ、七つ、八つ、九つ、十 (とお) — and it stops at ten; beyond that you must switch. 個 (こ) is the Sino-Japanese generic for small solid objects and continues indefinitely: 卵十個、りんご三個 are both fine. In shops you'll hear 個 more for packaged goods, つ more in homes and restaurants: 「餃子を二つください» at a counter, 「卵を二個» sounds slightly technical.

Age uses the same native system historically — 二十歳 is はたち, the fossil of that series. Abstract things (ideas, reasons, questions) take つ comfortably: 「質問が二つあります». When a specific counter exists (books 冊, bottles 本), natives prefer it, but つ/個 is the universal spare tyre — every learner should keep it inflated for the day the exact counter won't come to mind.
I'm reading the notice on my apartment building's board: «ゴミは指定の袋に入れ、収集日の朝8時までに出してください。粗大ゴミは事前に申し込みが必要です。ご協力をお願いいたします。» Translate and explain the register.

Translation: 'Please put rubbish in the designated bags and put it out by 8 a.m. on collection day. Oversized rubbish requires an application in advance. Thank you for your cooperation.' Practical notes: 指定の袋 means your city sells official bags you must buy — the wrong bag is left behind with a sticker. 粗大ゴミ (bulky waste: furniture, appliances) needs a paid reservation and a sticker （粗大ゴミシール) in most cities.

The register is classic public-notice Japanese: imperatives softened into requests — 出してください instead of 出せ, and the closing formula ご協力をお願いいたします (humble いたす) that ends nearly every notice in Japan, from train posters to tax letters. Other notice words you'll meet: 立入禁止 (no entry), お静かに (please be quiet), 関係者以外 (authorised persons only), 〜はご遠慮ください (please refrain from —, the polite way to ban smoking, photos, and phone calls). Reading notices is the highest-value literacy in daily Japanese life.
Talking about my own family to my Japanese teacher, I said «私のお父さんは銀行員です» and she corrected it to 父. But at home I call him お父さん. Explain the two vocabularies.

Japanese has humble in-group words for your own family used when speaking to outsiders: 父 (ちち) father, 母 (はは) mother, 兄 (あに) older brother, 姉 (あね) older sister, 弟、妹 keep the same forms, 夫 (おっと) husband, 妻 (つま) wife, 息子、娘. The お〜さん forms — お父さん、お母さん — are for addressing your own family members directly, and for referring to other people's family: 「田中さんのお父さん».

So to your teacher: 「父は銀行員です». Calling him お父さん in that sentence elevates your own family before an outsider — the same uchi/soto logic as dropping your boss's title to a client. Direct address is the exception: at home, お父さん is right, and 父 would be bizarrely cold to his face. Modern drift exists — young speakers increasingly say うちのお父さん casually even to friends — but in any formal or examined context, the humble set is required. Learn family words as pairs: ちち/おとうさん, はは/おかあさん, and mark every pair 'mine' vs 'yours/theirs'.
Money readings trip me: the total was «一万二千三百円» and I froze. How does Japanese counting group digits, and what do I say handing over a 10,000 yen note?

Japanese groups large numbers by 万 (ten thousand), not by thousands: 一万二千三百円 = 12,300 yen — literally 'one ten-thousand, two thousand, three hundred'. So 100,000 is 十万 (ten ten-thousands), a million is 百万, and a hundred million is 一億. Convert by re-chunking into fours: 12,300 → 1|2300 → 一万二千三百. Prices are usually written in Arabic numerals in shops, but spoken totals, news, and salaries run on 万 — rent of 十五万円 is 150,000 yen a month.

Handing over a 10,000-yen note for a small purchase, the clerk may ask 「大きい方でよろしいですか» (is the large note OK?) — answer 「はい、大丈夫です». The note itself is 一万円札 (いちまんえんさつ). Counting money aloud at the register: coins by 枚? No — money amounts are just 円 amounts; 枚 is for the physical notes if you must count them. Practise by reading your rent, salary, and phone price in 万 until the re-chunking is automatic.
The weather app says: «明日は曇りのち雨。降水確率70%。最高気温18度、最低気温11度でしょう。» I get the gist but want the grammar of forecasts.

Forecast Japanese is compressed noun-phrases. 曇りのち雨 = 'cloudy, later rain' — のち means 'afterwards' and chains weather like beads: 晴れのち曇り (fine, later cloudy), 雨時々曇り (rain, at times cloudy — 時々 = occasionally), 曇り一時雨 (cloudy, rain for a time — 一時 = temporarily). 降水確率70% is the probability of precipitation, read こうすいかくりつ.

最高気温/最低気温 are the high and low; 度 (ど) is degrees. The でしょう at the end is the forecaster's hedge — 'it will probably be' — because even the weather bureau doesn't state the future flatly. Listen for regional frames on TV: 「関東地方は» (in the Kanto region), 「沿岸部では» (in coastal areas), and warnings escalate from 注意報 (advisory) to 警報 (warning) to 特別警報 (emergency warning) — three words worth recognising instantly in typhoon season.
At the platform I heard: «まもなく、2番線に電車がまいります。白線の内側までお下がりください。» What is まいります doing here, and what's the 白線?

まいります is the humble form of 来る/行く doing announcement duty: 'a train will arrive shortly on platform 2'. Announcements use humble verbs for the company's own trains and staff — the railway lowers itself before passengers. まもなく means 'in a moment, shortly' and is the signature opening of station announcements nationwide.

白線 is the white line painted along the platform edge; 内側 is its station-side. 'Please step back behind the white line' — お下がりください uses the honorific お〜ください pattern for passengers. Related announcements to bank: 「足元にご注意ください» (mind your step/the gap), 「駆け込み乗車はおやめください» (please don't rush the doors — 駆け込み乗車 is the running-for-the-train dash), 「この電車は回送です» (this train is out of service — 回送 cars pass through or stop but don't board). Once you know the twenty fixed lines, Japanese stations become free listening practice.
Restaurant in Kyoto: what do I say to ask for the bill, to ask if I can pay by card, and what will the server say when bringing dishes?

For the bill: 「お会計をお願いします» — お会計 (the bill/check) with the beautifying お, or catch an eye and make the writing gesture; the phrase is politer. Card: 「カードで払えますか» or more politely 「カードは使えますか». When you're seated you may hear 「お水でよろしいですか» (is water all right?) and the server bringing dishes says 「お待たせいたしました。こちら、〜でございます» — でございます is the extra-polite form of です used for presenting things to customers.

Ordering politely: 「〜をください» is fine; 「〜をお願いします» is softer and very common. To call staff: 「すみません» — never a raised hand snap; a gentle すみません with eye contact. Kyoto colour: some traditional places use おおきに for 'thank you' (Kansai dialect) — you'll hear it from older staff; respond with a smile and ありがとうございます, don't try to perform the dialect back. At the door, staff send you off with 「ありがとうございました。またお越しください» — the past-tense thank-you again, because the meal is complete.
Buildings: how do I ask which floor the pharmacy is on, and say my office is on the seventh floor? I heard «なんがい» and something about basements.

Floors are counted with 階 (かい/がい): 「薬局は何階ですか» — 何階 is read なんがい here (the counter voices after なん). 'My office is on the seventh floor': 「私の事務所は七階にあります» — 七階 is ななかい. Watch the irregulars: 一階 いっかい, 三階 さんがい, 六階 ろっかい, 八階 はっかい/はちかい, 十階 じっかい/じゅっかい.

Basements take 地下 + number + 階: 「地下二階» (ちかにかい), abbreviated B2 on signs, just as 地上 floors show as 7F. Supermarkets and food halls love the basement — デパ地下 (department store basement food floor) is a destination in itself. In lifts, staff may announce 「七階でございます» as the doors open. One counting caution: Japanese 一階 is the ground floor (like British usage), so an American 'second floor' is 二階 — off-by-one errors in meeting points come from exactly this.
Why «雨が降っている» and «風が強い» — why が with weather? And «桜が咲く» — nobody chose these topics, so why not は?

Because が also marks the subject of a phenomenon you're presenting as new information or observing in the moment. Weather sentences report what's happening now: 「雨が降っています», 「風が強くなってきました». The rain isn't an established topic you're commenting on — it's the event itself. Same with natural processes: 「桜が咲きました» announces the blossoms have bloomed.

は steps in when the phenomenon becomes the topic of a general statement: 「雨は嫌いです» (rain — as a category — I dislike), 「今年の桜は早い» (this year's blossoms, as our topic, are early). This is the neutral-description use of が that grammars call 現象文 (phenomenon sentences): pure presentation, no topic yet. It's also why stories open with が — 「昔々、おじいさんがいました» presents the old man for the first time; once he's established, the narration switches to は. First mention が, continuing topic は — that single rhythm underlies most of the は/が mystery.
«千円しかありません» — why does しか need a negative verb, and how is it different from «千円だけあります»?

しか is a negative-polarity word: it only works with a negative ending, and together they mean 'only' with a flavour of 'not enough / less than hoped'. 「千円しかありません» = I have only 1,000 yen (and that's a problem). 「千円だけあります» with だけ is neutral: I have exactly 1,000 yen — could be plenty if the coffee costs 800.

So the pair しか〜ない vs だけ is evaluation, not quantity: the same amount, framed as scarcity or as simple fact. Common frames: 「一人しか来なかった» (only one person came — disappointing), 「寝るしかない» (there's nothing for it but to sleep — resignation), 「やるしかない» (just have to do it). Learner error to avoid: ✕しかあります. And in casual speech the negative can be shortened: 「千円しかない». When you want 'only' without the sigh, use だけ; when the sigh is the point, しか〜ない.
My friend texts: «それ食べちゃった。明日行かなきゃ。わかんない。」 My dictionary can't find ちゃった、なきゃ、わかんない anywhere.

These are casual contractions — spoken forms that dictionaries list under their full shapes. 食べちゃった = 食べてしまった (ate it up / went and ate it — しまう adds a note of completion or mild regret). 行かなきゃ = 行かなければならない shortened twice (have to go). わかんない = 分からない with the ら dropped, the standard casual pronunciation.

The productive sets: てしまう → ちゃう (and でしまう → じゃう: 飲んじゃった), なければならない → なきゃ, なければ → なければ→なきゃ, ては → ちゃ (しちゃだめ = don't do it), のだ → んだ （行くんだ), という → って. You'll also hear particles dropped entirely between friends: 「これ、食べる?» Register warning: these forms are for friends, family, and your own diary — messages to a teacher or boss keep the full shapes. But listening comprehension depends on them; nobody actually speaks in textbook sentences.
Addressing a letter and a parcel in Japan: when do I write 様、殿、御中、行? My office gets mail addressed to «営業部御中» and to me personally as «山田様».

The suffix system: 様 is the standard honorific for a named individual — 「山田様» on your mail is correct and neutral-polite. 御中 (おんちゅう) is for an organisation or department with no named person: 「営業部御中» = 'To the Sales Department'. Never combine them for one addressee — a letter to a person inside a department is 「営業部 山田様», not 御中 plus 様.

殿 is for documents downward or between officials — certificates, internal notices; in modern business it's largely avoided externally because it can read as looking down. On envelopes you'll also see the correction system: if a printed name ends with 行 (to) or 宛， the sender strikes it out and writes 様 when replying — pre-printed 行 is a humble 'to' the sender applies to themselves. And 先生 for teachers/doctors/lawyers replaces 様 in most contexts: 「佐藤先生». Master 様 and 御中 and you can address 95% of Japanese mail correctly.
How do I ask permission very politely — 'May I take a photo here?', 'May I sit here?', 'May I open the window?' — for a formal tour setting?

The frame is て-form + もよろしいでしょうか: 「ここで写真を撮ってもよろしいでしょうか», 「ここに座ってもよろしいでしょうか», 「窓を開けてもよろしいでしょうか». よろしい is the formal counterpart of いい; でしょうか softens the question into a consultation. In everyday polite speech もいいですか suffices; on a formal tour, よろしいでしょうか is the register that matches the setting.

Expect answers in kind: permission is granted with 「どうぞ» or 「はい、結構です» (結構です here = that's fine — though the same words with a headshake mean 'no thank you', context and tone decide). A refusal is rarely a flat no; listen for 「申し訳ございませんが、こちらは撮影禁止となっております» (I'm sorry, photography is prohibited here) — となっております states a rule, not a personal refusal, which is how Japanese institutions say no without anyone losing face. Noticing that indirection is half of formal listening comprehension.
My business Japanese teacher says I overuse させていただく. When is it actually correct, and what should I say instead in the wrong cases?

させていただく means 'I humbly receive the favour of being allowed to do X' — it needs, logically, someone whose permission or goodwill makes your action possible. Correct: 「ご説明させていただきます» (explaining to the client who grants you the floor), 「本日は休業させていただきます» (a shop closing — customers' indulgence is genuinely involved), 「参加させていただきます» (joining an event by invitation).

Overuse cases: announcing your own unilateral acts as if permitted — ✕「電車に乗らせていただきます» to no one in particular, or using it for obligations: ✕「提出させていただきます» for a report you simply must submit (just say 提出いたします). The clean replacements are the humble いたす-forms: ご連絡いたします、確認いたします、対応いたします. The modern inflation of させていただく is so discussed that it has a nickname — させていただく症候群. Rule: if you can't name whose favour you're receiving, drop it and use いたします. Your teacher's ear is right; restraint with this form is a marker of genuinely polished business Japanese.
Why do Japanese train and shop announcements say things twice — once in keigo-heavy Japanese and once in simple English — and what's «お客様» doing grammatically?

お客様 is the honorific word for customer/guest — 客 (customer) wrapped in お〜様. Announcements address the crowd as お客様 because every listener is, institutionally, a guest being served: 「お客様にお知らせいたします» (we humbly inform our customers). You'll also hear 皆様 (everyone, honorific) in stations and theatres. The grammar point: お客様 is treated as an elevated third person — verbs about them take honorific forms: 「お客様がお待ちです» (a customer is waiting — said to staff about the client, with お待ち being the honorific pattern).

The double announcement reflects service culture plus practicality: the Japanese version performs the full courtesy the setting demands (and carries the precise detail — platform numbers, car positions), while the English is a compressed functional summary. If you understand the Japanese, you'll notice the English often omits the reason and the apology. Listening strategy: train your ear on the Japanese first — it's formulaic, slow, and repeated daily, making announcements the best free keigo tutor in the country.
